body.heading: Journeys written into the year
paragraphs: Migration is the regular, seasonal movement of animals between two habitats — typically to feed where food is plentiful and breed where conditions suit their young. It is one of the great spectacles of nature: billions of birds, fish, insects and mammals on the move each year.

The champion is the Arctic tern, which flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year — a round trip of roughly 70,000 kilometres, chasing an endless summer and living, in effect, through two summers a year.

body.heading: How they find the way
paragraphs: Migrants navigate with a toolkit no single sense explains. Birds use the Sun and stars as compasses, follow coastlines, rivers and other landmarks, and can sense Earth's magnetic field — an inbuilt compass that works even under cloud. Salmon add smell, homing to the exact river where they were born.

The fuel is fat. Before departure, migrants gorge and may nearly double their weight; some small birds then fly for days without stopping. Monarch butterflies do the trip in relays — no single butterfly makes the whole return journey; its grandchildren finish it.

body.heading: Why the effort pays
paragraphs: Migration is dangerous and exhausting, so the payoff must be large: rich seasonal food, safer breeding grounds, escape from winter cold or drought. The Serengeti's wildebeest herds — over a million animals — follow the rains and the fresh grass they bring.

The journeys also connect ecosystems. Salmon carry ocean nutrients into forests; migrant birds move seeds and insects' eggs between continents. A migrant is a thread stitching distant habitats together. Break one link in the route — a drained wetland, a blocked river — and the whole journey can fail.

takeaway: Migration is the seasonal movement of animals between habitats, guided by the Sun, stars, landmarks and Earth's magnetic field, and powered by stored fat.
